name: Transformers.js SegFormer semantic segmentation (ADE20K)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004'). Model weights are a separate licence: nvidia/segformer-b0-finetuned-ade-512-512 points to the NVIDIA Source Code License for SegFormer, section 3.3 'non-commercially ... research or evaluation purposes only'.
what_it_does: Runs SegFormer-B0 (ADE20K, 150 classes) in the browser and returns a per-pixel class map whose labels include wall, building, sky, windowpane, house, road, car and tree.
input_output: Input: RawImage / URL / canvas (RGB). Processor output: pixel_values Tensor[1,3,512,512]. Pipeline output: Array<{label: string, score: null, mask: RawImage}>; mask is one-channel 0/255 at target_sizes.
why_critical_for_this_project: scene-parse: replaces the hand-built class map in src/scene-parse.js with a published 150-class model that actually has `building` and `windowpane`. COCO does not (verified: the EfficientDet-Lite0 TFLite label list has no building, window or sky). This is the single largest upgrade for the project's weakest layer.
maturity_evidence: SegFormer, Xie et al., NeurIPS 2021; nvidia/segformer-b0-finetuned-ade-512-512 has 330,689 Hugging Face downloads (API, 2026-10-17); ADE20K is the standard 150-class segmentation benchmark; transformers.js 4.3.1 is a tagged release. The model's own id2label list names wall, building, sky, windowpane, house, skyscraper, road, car, tree.
integration_note: Browser ESM: npm `@huggingface/transformers` or a CDN import; ONNX Runtime Web WASM/WebGPU. Model download is the cost (SegFormer-B0 ONNX is tens of MB). Licence constraint: code Apache-2.0, weights non-commercial (NVIDIA), so this is research/evaluation unless the weights are replaced with a permissively licensed checkpoint.
risks: Weights are non-commercial; fixed 512x512 resize distorts perspective; 150-class label noise (a wall can be labelled building and vice versa); first load downloads a model; browser memory/WASM startup; deterministic only if the ORT session is pinned (see onnxruntime-session-options).

name: Skyline extraction with a fine-tuned OneFormer
licence: GPL-3.0 (LICENSE: 'GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007').
what_it_does: Segments sky versus foreground with a OneFormer ADE20K checkpoint fine-tuned on GeoPose3K and returns a skyline/label mask for mountainous imagery.
key_api:
from SkylineExtraction.OneFormer import SkylinePipeline
pipe = SkylinePipeline(device=torch.device('cuda'))
mask = pipe.run_inference(image)  # image: np.ndarray HxWx3, RGB uint8
# default checkpoint = PRE_TRAINED_CHECKPOINT
#   mieszkok/shi-labs_oneformer_ade20k_swin_large_geopose3k_original_images900_epochs5
snippet:
panoptic_inputs = self.processor(images=image, task_inputs=["panoptic"], return_tensors="pt")
        panoptic_inputs = {k: v.to(self.device) for k, v in panoptic_inputs.items()}

        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = self.model(**panoptic_inputs)
        panoptic_segmentation = self.processor.post_process_panoptic_segmentation(outputs, target_sizes=[
            (image.shape[0], image.shape[1])])[0]
        mask = SkylinePipeline.post_process_panoptic_segmentation(
            panoptic_segmentation['segmentation'],
            [SegmentsInfo.from_dict(d) for d in panoptic_segmentation['segments_info']],
        )
        return mask
input_output: Input: HxWx3 RGB uint8 numpy array. Output: HxW label map (panoptic segment ids remapped to label ids); skyline is derived from the sky/foreground boundary.
why_critical_for_this_project: horizon: gives a learned skyline instead of the hand-picked sky band and threshold constants in src/sky.js; the horizon row can be read from the mask instead of guessed.
maturity_evidence: OneFormer, Shi et al., CVPR 2023; ADE20K-pretrained Swin-Large backbone; fine-tuned on the first 900 GeoPose3K images (repo README). The wrapper itself is a single-author project, so the evidence is the paper + backbone, not adoption of this repo.
integration_note: PyTorch only; not browser. GPL-3.0 means a derivative integrated into DVOR-8 must be GPL-compatible. Export to ONNX or reproduce the sky class with the Apache/non-commercial SegFormer route instead.
risks: GPL-3.0; PyTorch + GPU; mountainous-domain training (yards and streets differ); large checkpoint; unmaintained single-author wrapper; sky class index must be read from the checkpoint, not assumed.

name: Window detection in facades using heatmap fusion
licence: MIT (LICENSE: 'MIT License Copyright (c) 2020 chuankang li').
what_it_does: Locates window-corner keypoints on a facade as heatmaps, groups the four corners into window quadrilaterals, and optionally rectifies them.
key_api:
python infer.py --cfg /path/to/config.yaml --model /path/to/model.tar --infer /path/to/images
# core grouping API:
group_corners_on_tags(idx, parser, dets, tags, patch_width, patch_height,
                      im_width, im_height, rectify, winScoreThres) -> list[dict]
snippet:
# rescale ratio from patch size to image size
    ratio = max(im_width, im_height) / patch_height
    ratio = np.array([ratio, ratio])

    grouped = parser.parse(np.float32(dets), np.float32(tags), idx, ratio, rectify)  # shape=(num_of_windows, 4, 4)

    linked_window = list() # convert format & do rectify
    for n_w in range(len(grouped)):
        score = np.mean(grouped[n_w][:,2])
        if score < winScoreThres: #skip low-score windows
            continue
        linked_window.append(convert_to_dict(grouped[n_w]))

    return linked_window
input_output: Input: facade RGB image; network outputs corner heatmaps and tag heatmaps. Output: a list of windows, each four corners (lt, lb, rb, rt) in image coordinates plus a mean score.
why_critical_for_this_project: facade-geometry: provides real window boxes for the facade grid instead of typed pitch/row constants; those boxes can seed the window sprites and the 'never outline a window' rule.
maturity_evidence: Peer-reviewed: Li et al., 'Window Detection in Facades Using Heatmap Fusion', Journal of Computer Science and Technology 35(4):900-912, 2020; reported precision 91.4% and recall 91.0% at IoU 0.5 on a 3,418-image ZJU facade dataset. MIT licence.
integration_note: PyTorch + custom C extensions; not browser. MIT permits porting the corner-grouping logic; for a browser pipeline export the backbone to ONNX or use the facade SegFormer mask plus projection profile.
risks: Old PyTorch code, CUDA assumptions, unmaintained; trained for rectified/frontal facades; window grouping needs a tuned score threshold; checkpoint is an external download.

name: SegFormer-B0 facade parser (CMP, 6 classes)
licence: MIT (model card metadata `license: mit`). Caveat: the model card says it starts from NVIDIA's ADE20K-pretrained SegFormer-B0; the base checkpoint's own licence is the non-commercial NVIDIA Source Code License, so the MIT claim covers this fine-tune only.
what_it_does: Segments a rectified facade into background, facade_wall, window, door, balcony and vegetation_occluder with a 3.7M-parameter SegFormer-B0.
snippet:
"id2label": {
    "0": "background",
    "1": "facade_wall",
    "2": "window",
    "3": "door",
    "4": "balcony",
    "5": "vegetation_occluder"
input_output: Input: rectified facade RGB image. Output: HxW class ids 0-5 (or one binary mask per present label via the pipeline).
why_critical_for_this_project: facade-geometry: returns window and wall masks directly, which is exactly the geometry the facade layer needs; replaces thresholding and hand-tuned window colours.
maturity_evidence: CMP Facade Database (378 train / 114 test rectified facades); model card reports mean IoU 0.4856, facade_wall IoU 0.867, window IoU 0.410, door IoU 0.460, balcony IoU 0.230. No peer-reviewed paper for this fine-tune; single author.
integration_note: Browser ESM through transformers.js; MIT metadata; 512x512 input. Licence constraint: the base weights' non-commercial terms must be checked before commercial use.
risks: Window IoU is only 0.410; trained on rectified frontal facades, so perspective yard photos will degrade; single-author, no paper; class imbalance; base-weights provenance.

name: 1-D projection-profile segmentation
licence: MIT (LICENSE: 'MIT License Copyright (c) 2019 Lars Vögtlin').
what_it_does: Computes a 1-D projection profile by summing an image along one axis and splits the profile into runs above a threshold; the standard projection-profile primitive for row/column spacing.
key_api:
getVerticalProjectionProfile(img) -> np.ndarray   # np.sum(img, axis=0)
cutWordImages(profiles, img, threshold, line_threshold,
              output_folder, img_name, extension)   # threshold is a sum-of-pixels cutoff
input_output: Input: 2-D grayscale/binary array. Output: a 1-D profile, then intervals [start,end] where the profile stays above threshold for longer than line_threshold.
why_critical_for_this_project: facade-geometry: the missing 1-D step for window pitch. Apply it to the column sums of a window mask or vertical-edge map to recover bay spacing and row spacing instead of the hand-picked pitch constants.
maturity_evidence: Projection-profile segmentation is a textbook document-analysis method; this repo is a small 2019 MIT CLI (single author, no paper, no tests), so it is a reference implementation rather than a maintained dependency.
integration_note: Port the 14-line loop to JS; MIT; no dependencies. It is domain-generic, so the facade-specific work (which projection, which threshold) stays ours.
risks: Not facade-specific; threshold and minimum-run length are hand-set; no tests; unmaintained; a projection profile alone cannot distinguish a window row from a balcony rail.

name: PixelOE pixelize pipeline
version_or_commit: 1.0.0 (PyPI sdist; repository version is 1.0.1 and its layout changed)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Contrast-aware pixelization: resize, outline-expand, colour-match, contrast-based downsample, and optional palette quantisation.
key_api:
pixelize(img,
        mode="contrast", target_size=128, patch_size=16, pixel_size=None,
        thickness=2, color_matching=True, contrast=1.0, saturation=1.0,
        colors=None, color_quant_method="kmeans", colors_with_weight=False,
        no_upscale=False, no_downscale=False)
snippet:
def pixelize(
    img,
    mode="contrast",
    target_size=128,
    patch_size=16,
    pixel_size=None,
    thickness=2,
    color_matching=True,
    contrast=1.0,
    saturation=1.0,
    colors=None,
    color_quant_method="kmeans",
    colors_with_weight=False,
    no_upscale=False,
    no_downscale=False,
input_output: Input: BGR uint8 HxWx3. Output: BGR uint8 pixel-art image at the computed target size; optional palette/quantised output.
why_critical_for_this_project: reduction: the published replacement for the area-mean 5x5 block reduction. Its stage 1 (outline expansion) is specifically designed so fine details survive downscaling, which is the project's documented 'windows melt / road markings vanish' fault.
maturity_evidence: PixelOE 1.0.0 on PyPI; the repository ships ComfyUI custom nodes (README); the outline-expansion stage is evaluated against 'Make Your Own Sprites: Aliasing-Aware and Cell-Controllable Pixelization' (SIGGRAPH Asia 2022) in the README.
integration_note: Python/OpenCV/Torch; not browser. Port the outline expansion and `find_pixel` to JS (Apache-2.0 permits it), or run it offline as a reference generator for tests.
risks: Python + Torch dependency for the median filters; `target_size` semantics differ from a fixed 5x5 cell; k-means quantisation is not deterministic without a seed; upscaling defaults can hide detail loss.

name: PixelOE contrast-based downscale (`find_pixel`)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Chooses the minimum, maximum, or centre value of each patch from the patch's median/mean skew, so dark or bright detail is kept instead of averaged away.
key_api:
find_pixel(chunks)  # chunks: patch tensor; returns one LAB value per patch
contrast_based_downscale(img, target_size=128)  # img: BGR uint8
snippet:
def find_pixel(chunks):
    mid = chunks[..., chunks.shape[-1] // 2][..., None]
    med = torch.median(chunks, dim=1, keepdims=True).values
    mu = torch.mean(chunks, dim=1, keepdims=True)
    maxi = torch.max(chunks, dim=1, keepdims=True).values
    mini = torch.min(chunks, dim=1, keepdims=True).values

    output = mid
    mini_loc = (med < mu) & (maxi - med > med - mini)
    maxi_loc = (med > mu) & (maxi - med < med - mini)

    output[mini_loc] = mini[mini_loc]
    output[maxi_loc] = maxi[maxi_loc]

    return output
input_output: Input: BGR uint8 image, target size. Internal: LAB patches. Output: BGR uint8 image at target_hw, using nearest-neighbour for the final resize.
why_critical_for_this_project: reduction: this is the exact algorithm that makes a 1-px dark line survive a patch reduction. It replaces `Math.round(sum/count)` in the block reducer and is small enough to port verbatim.
maturity_evidence: PixelOE 1.0.0 (PyPI), Apache-2.0; the method is the 'contrast-based downsampling' stage of the PixelOE pipeline whose outline expansion is evaluated in the SIGGRAPH Asia 2022 pixelization paper (README).
integration_note: Port `find_pixel` to JS typed arrays; Apache-2.0; no native dependency in the port. Keep LAB conversion in the port (sRGB -> XYZ -> LAB) or use the project's existing linear-light code.
risks: The condition `maxi - med == med - mini` falls back to the midpoint; patch edge handling is not specified for non-divisible sizes; the A and B LAB channels are always median-filtered while L uses the skew rule; results depend on the LAB conversion constants.

name: image2pixel-web browser pixel-art pipeline
licence: Custom Restricted License (LICENSE: 'use the Software for personal, educational, or non-commercial purposes only'; 'Commercial use ... strictly prohibited without explicit written permission'). Not an OSI licence.
what_it_does: A working browser pixel-art converter: block average or centre sampling, median cut in RGB/LAB, LAB nearest-colour matching, and Floyd–Steinberg dithering.
key_api:
processWithClassicLab(imageData, blockSize, palette)
medianCutGetPaletteInLab(imageData, colorCount)
extractBlockGridAverage(imageData, blockSize) -> {grid, cols, rows}
nearestLabColor(r, g, b, labPalette) -> [r,g,b]
input_output: Input: ImageData + blockSize (2-20) + palette [[r,g,b],...]. Output: ImageData at block resolution.
why_critical_for_this_project: reduction/palette: the closest existing browser implementation to the current pipeline, useful as an A/B baseline. Its block average is exactly the operation that destroys 1-px structure, so the database records it as the thing to replace, not the fix.
maturity_evidence: Live product image2pixel.app with iOS/Android/Steam/Chrome listings (README); five documented algorithms and built-in palettes. No releases, no tests, no open licence.
integration_note: Browser, no build step; but the licence forbids commercial use and competing derivative works, so DVOR-8 must not vendor it. Read it as a reference, or re-implement the LAB median cut (the math is standard).
risks: Non-commercial custom licence; block average loses detail; no tests; the licence blocks reuse; no source maps.

name: libimagequant (pngquant quantizer)
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (COPYRIGHT: 'libimagequant ... contains extensive changes and additions by Kornel Lesiński licensed under GPL v3 or later').
what_it_does: High-quality palette quantisation with median cut plus k-means refinement, perceptual colour space, dithering and alpha support.
input_output: Input: RGBA8 bitmap + options. Output: palette (RGBA) + one index per pixel (or a remapped RGBA image with dithering).
why_critical_for_this_project: palette: the strongest published quantiser to replace the fixed 28-colour median-cut table; its k-means refinement and perceptual distance are the quality bar for palette gates.
maturity_evidence: libimagequant is pngquant's quantiser (pngquant.org/lib); version 4.4.1; Pillow exposes it as `Quantize.LIBIMAGEQUANT` (Pillow 13.0.0 docs/source), which is independent evidence of adoption beyond the repo itself.
integration_note: Native C/Rust, not browser. Build to WASM or call the pngquant CLI offline; GPL-3.0-or-later contaminates a distributed derivative, so keep it at arm's length (CLI / build-time asset) unless the project is GPL.
risks: GPL-3.0+; native build; Rust toolchain; determinism of k-means refinement must be checked; WASM build size; gamma and alpha handling are subtle.

name: Pillow median-cut quantizer
licence: MIT-CMU / HPND (LICENSE: 'Pillow is licensed under the open source MIT-CMU License').
what_it_does: Median-cut palette generation with optional k-means refinement, plus maximum-coverage, fast-octree and libimagequant backends.
key_api:
Image.quantize(colors=256, method=None, kmeans=0, palette=None,
               dither=Dither.FLOYDSTEINBERG)
# method=None -> Quantize.MEDIANCUT for RGB; Quantize.FASTOCTREE for RGBA
# colors default 256; kmeans 0 = off; dither default Floyd–Steinberg
input_output: Input: RGB/RGBA image. Output: P-mode image (palette + indices).
why_critical_for_this_project: palette: the reference implementation for the median-cut route already in src/palette.js; its C code shows the box-splitting rule and its Python API supplies the exact defaults and k-means switch.
maturity_evidence: Pillow 13.0.0 is the standard Python imaging library; the median-cut implementation is in its C core and `Image.quantize` documents the default method. libimagequant support in Pillow is separately documented.
integration_note: Python only. Port the median-cut box split to JS (the project already has a median cut); MIT-CMU licence permits it. Do not depend on Pillow at runtime.
risks: Python/C extension; median cut is lower quality than libimagequant; dithering default changes the output; k-means >0 changes cost and determinism; palette size >256 rejected.

name: image-q NeuQuant (JavaScript port)
licence: MIT (packages/image-q/package.json: 'license': 'MIT'; LICENSE in the package).
what_it_does: NeuQuant neural-network colour quantisation (Dekker 1994) in TypeScript, with pluggable colour-distance metrics and a browser ESM build.
input_output: Input: PointContainer of RGBA points (an image). Output: Palette (array of RGBA points) via a generator that yields progress.
why_critical_for_this_project: palette: a browser-capable, seeded-by-data alternative to median cut/k-means; NeuQuant's fixed network size (256 default) makes the 28-colour budget explicit and gives a second quantiser for palette gates.
maturity_evidence: NeuQuant by Anthony Dekker, 'Kohonen neural networks for optimal colour quantization', Network: Computation in Neural Systems 5 (1994) 351-367, quoted in the file header; image-q 3.0.4 tagged release; TypeScript port by Igor Bezkrovnyi (MIT).
integration_note: Browser ESM via the package's `dist/esm` build (bundler) or Node; MIT. It is a library, not a drop-in script, so a small adapter is needed.
risks: NeuQuant is lower quality than libimagequant; 256-network default must be lowered to 28; no worker; the 50MB repo is large to vendor; quantize() is a generator and must be drained.

name: Lospec palette data: Endesga 32 (JSON and GIMP .gpl)
version_or_commit: palette snapshot fetched 2026-10-17; 32 colours; no upstream version
licence: No licence stated on the palette page or the JSON endpoint. The file credits author ENDESGA and says it was created for NYKRA. Treat as attribution-only community data and confirm reuse terms before redistribution; the .gpl text format itself is a de-facto standard and is not licensed by this palette.
language: Data: JSON and GIMP Palette text
what_it_does: A 32-colour pixel-art palette and the two interchange forms Lospec serves: JSON `{name, author, colors:[hex]}` and GIMP `.gpl` (RGB triples with a hex name). Aseprite extends `.gpl` with `Channels: RGBA` plus a fourth alpha column.
key_api:
GET https://lospec.com/palette-list/endesga-32.json
  -> {"name":"Endesga 32","author":"ENDESGA","colors":["be4a2f", ... 32 hexes]}
GET https://lospec.com/palette-list/endesga-32.gpl
  -> "GIMP Palette" / "#Palette Name: ..." / "R G B hex" lines
Aseprite .gpl extension: header "GIMP Palette", "Channels: RGBA", then "R G B A name".
snippet: GIMP Palette #Palette Name: Endesga 32 #Description: Originally created for NYKRA. #Colors: 32 190 74 47 be4a2f 215 118 67 d77643 234 212 170 ead4aa 228 166 114 e4a672 184 111 80 b86f50 115 62 57 733e39 62 39 49 3e2731 162 38 51 a22633
input_output: HTTP GET -> JSON palette (32 hex strings) or text .gpl (32 RGB triples). Output: a palette table of 32 RGB colours.
why_critical_for_this_project: palette: the published palette the project's ramps imitate. It gives a fixed, recognisable 32-colour target and a real interchange format, so palette gates can compare against a named standard instead of a hand-picked table.
maturity_evidence: Lospec is the community's palette archive; Endesga 32 is credited to ENDESGA and was created for NYKRA (palette description); the .gpl format is implemented by GIMP, Aseprite and Lospec. There is no release or formal licence.
integration_note: Fetch or embed the JSON/GPL; browser no-build. Licence constraint: no explicit palette licence, so attribute ENDESGA/Lospec and verify before shipping. The 32 values are data, not code.
risks: No explicit licence; endpoint can change; 32 colours may be too coarse or too stylised for a photograph; `.gpl` names are cosmetic and should not be used as semantic labels.

name: IBM CGA 16-colour palette (MIT table)
licence: MIT (LICENSE.md: 'MIT License Copyright (c) 2021-2024 Ben Hendel-Doying').
what_it_does: The 16 IBM CGA/EGA default colours as a static table with 0xAA/0x55/0xFF channel levels.
key_api:
CGA16.Black, CGA16.Blue, CGA16.Green, CGA16.Cyan,
CGA16.Red, CGA16.Magenta, CGA16.Brown, CGA16.LightGray,
CGA16.DarkGray, CGA16.BrightBlue, CGA16.BrightGreen, CGA16.BrightCyan,
CGA16.BrightRed, CGA16.BrightMagenta, CGA16.Yellow, CGA16.White
input_output: Static data: 16 `Color` values (RGB bytes).
why_critical_for_this_project: palette: a hardware-authentic 16-colour constraint for the 8-bit look; a second, very small palette for collapse/flatness gates and for testing whether the frame survives at CGA depth.
maturity_evidence: IBM CGA/EGA standard 16-colour default palette; the table cites ModdingWiki's EGA Palette page; MIT repo. It is a data table, not an algorithm, so maturity is the standard itself.
integration_note: Copy the 16 hex values into JS; MIT. No runtime dependency.
risks: CGA vs EGA naming; 16 colours is very coarse for a photograph; the table uses the 0xAA/0x55/0xFF EGA levels, not the 2-bit RGBI bit pattern.

name: PixelOE LAB/wavelet colour matching
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Matches a generated image's LAB mean and standard deviation to a source image, then restores the source's low-frequency colour with a wavelet decomposition.
key_api:
match_color(source, target, level=5)  # BGR uint8 -> BGR uint8
wavelet_colorfix(inp, target, level=5)
wavelet_decomposition(inp, levels)
snippet:
# Convert RGB to L*a*b*, and then match the std/mean
    source_lab = cv2.cvtColor(source, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB).astype(np.float32) / 255
    target_lab = cv2.cvtColor(target, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB).astype(np.float32) / 255
    result = (source_lab - np.mean(source_lab)) / np.std(source_lab)
    result = result * np.std(target_lab) + np.mean(target_lab)
    source = cv2.cvtColor(
        (result * 255).clip(0, 255).astype(np.uint8), cv2.COLOR_LAB2BGR
    )

    source = source.astype(np.float32)
    # Use wavelet colorfix method to match original low frequency data at first
    source[:, :, 0] = wavelet_colorfix(source[:, :, 0], target[:, :, 0], level=level)
    source[:, :, 1] = wavelet_colorfix(source[:, :, 1], target[:, :, 1], level=level)
    source[:, :, 2] = wavelet_colorfix(source[:, :, 2], target[:, :, 2], level=level)
    output = source
input_output: Input: source and target BGR uint8 images (same size after resize). Output: source with target's LAB statistics and low-frequency colour.
why_critical_for_this_project: style-register: directly addresses the measured 'the frame is neutral where the accepted frame is blue' fault. The area-first reduction averages a region's colour; this is a published way to pull the reduced frame back to the photograph's colour distribution.
maturity_evidence: PixelOE 1.0.0 (PyPI), Apache-2.0; the same pipeline ships ComfyUI custom nodes; the low-frequency wavelet colour-fix is the standard colour-transfer step used in the project's reference pipeline.
integration_note: Python/OpenCV; port the mean/std LAB transfer and a small Gaussian pyramid to JS. Apache-2.0.
risks: Global mean/std can wash out local colour (a red car can still go neutral); wavelet level 5 is a tuned constant; source/target order is easy to reverse; not a substitute for per-region colour families.

name: MediaPipe Tasks Vision ObjectDetector (EfficientDet-Lite0)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Runs EfficientDet-Lite0 (COCO 80 classes) in the browser via WASM/GPU and returns bounding boxes, category names and scores.
input_output: Input: ImageSource. Output: ObjectDetectorResult = {detections: Detection[]}; each Detection has an optional BoundingBox and Category[] {score, index, categoryName, displayName}.
why_critical_for_this_project: objects: a real browser detector for cars, people, trucks and buses, replacing hand-coloured object heuristics. It also proves the COCO limit: the model's own label list contains no building, window or sky, which is why buildings must come from segmentation/structures, not COCO.
maturity_evidence: MediaPipe (Google), Apache-2.0; EfficientDet-Lite0 is the documented lightweight COCO detector; model file is 13MB TFLite; @mediapipe/tasks-vision 1.1.1. The model's embedded labels were read directly: person, bicycle, car ... toothbrush, with no building/window/sky.
integration_note: Browser ESM + WASM fileset (`@mediapipe/tasks-vision`); Apache-2.0. The WASM assets and the 13MB model must be hosted; no build step is possible for the model itself.
risks: COCO has no building class; 320x320 input misses small windows; boxes overlap; WASM/GPU backend differs; model download; not deterministic across backends.

name: @imgly/background-removal (mask to sprite)
licence: AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE.md: 'GNU Affero General Public License Version 3, 19 November 2007').
what_it_does: Runs an ONNX segmentation/matting model in the browser, writes its alpha mask into the image, and returns a transparent PNG/Blob — a complete mask-to-sprite path.
key_api:
removeBackground(image, configuration?) -> Promise<Blob>
segmentForeground(image, configuration?) -> Promise<Blob>
applySegmentationMask(image, mask, config?) -> Promise<Blob>
input_output: Input: ImageSource (URL/Blob/ImageData) + optional config. Output: Blob (PNG with alpha).
why_critical_for_this_project: objects: the mask-to-sprite mechanism. A car/person cut-out keeps the photograph's own pixels and gains alpha, which is precisely the 'photograph is a source of facts, not pixels' rule for movable objects.
maturity_evidence: IMG.LY production library, version 1.7.0; AGPL-3.0; runs an ONNX model fully client-side (README/package keywords 'image-segmentation', 'image-matting', 'onnx'). Maturity is commercial deployment, not a paper.
integration_note: Browser ESM; AGPL-3.0. Network use of AGPL code triggers a source-availability obligation; for a closed project use it offline as a comparison or replace it with a permissively licensed matting model.
risks: AGPL-3.0 is incompatible with a closed distribution; model download; GPU/WASM performance; alpha edges may fringe; output resolution is model-dependent; not deterministic across backends.

name: OpenCV morphological gradient (1-px outline)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Morphological gradient = dilate minus erode, the standard 1-px boundary operator for a binary or grayscale mask.
key_api:
cv2.morphologyEx(src, cv2.MORPH_GRADIENT, kernel,
                  anchor=(-1,-1), iterations=1,
                  borderType=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,
                  borderValue=cv2.morphologyDefaultBorderValue())
# default kernel if none: cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT, (3,3), (1,1))
input_output: Input: binary/grayscale (or colour) image + structuring element. Output: edge mask where dilate != erode; 1-px wide for a 3x3 kernel.
why_critical_for_this_project: outlines: the published 1-px boundary operator that replaces the hand-drawn outline pass. It follows any shape, so a building or car gets one outline that hugs its silhouette instead of a rectangle.
maturity_evidence: OpenCV 4.14.0, the reference computer-vision library; morphological gradient is a textbook operator (dilate − erode); PixelOE uses erode/dilate in its outline expansion.
integration_note: opencv.js WASM (~8MB) or port 3x3 erode/dilate to typed arrays; Apache-2.0. A 3x3 port is ~30 lines and avoids the WASM payload.
risks: opencv.js size; gradient on colour produces 3-channel edges; needs a binarised mask or it outlines texture; border handling can add a frame edge; OpenCV 5 API differs.

name: PixelOE contrast-aware outline expansion
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: Blends eroded and dilated copies weighted by local median-versus-min/max brightness, so bright/dark details survive before downscaling; returns the expanded image and a weight map.
key_api:
outline_expansion(img, erode=2, dilate=2, k=16, avg_scale=10, dist_scale=3)
    -> (img_out, weight)
expansion_weight(img, k=8, stride=2, avg_scale=10, dist_scale=3)
snippet:
def outline_expansion(img, erode=2, dilate=2, k=16, avg_scale=10, dist_scale=3):
    weight = expansion_weight(img, k, (k // 4) * 2, avg_scale, dist_scale)[..., None]
    orig_weight = sigmoid((weight - 0.5) * 5) * 0.25

    img_erode = img.copy()
    img_erode = cv2.erode(img_erode, kernel_expansion, iterations=erode).astype(
        np.float32
    )
    img_dilate = img.copy()
    img_dilate = cv2.dilate(img_dilate, kernel_expansion, iterations=dilate).astype(
        np.float32
    )

    output = img_erode * weight + img_dilate * (1 - weight)
    output = output * (1 - orig_weight) + img.astype(np.float32) * orig_weight
input_output: Input: BGR uint8 image. Output: BGR uint8 expanded image + float weight map (0..1).
why_critical_for_this_project: outlines/reduction: this is the published stage-1 that prevents a 1-px line from disappearing in the downscale. It is the direct fix for the measured 'area mean survives 0 of 8 cells' failure.
maturity_evidence: PixelOE 1.0.0 (PyPI), Apache-2.0; ComfyUI custom nodes in-repo; the README evaluates outline expansion against the SIGGRAPH Asia 2022 'Make Your Own Sprites' pixelization method.
integration_note: Python/OpenCV/Torch; port the erode/dilate blend and sigmoid weight to JS. Apache-2.0.
risks: Torch is used for median/max/min chunking; 9x9 kernels are tuned for pixel_size 6-16, not 5; parameters (avg_scale, dist_scale) are hand-tuned; can over-thicken dark edges.

name: Luanti falling-node support check
licence: LGPL-2.1-or-later (README badge `license-LGPLv2.1%2B`); textures/sounds separately CC BY-SA 3.0 in LICENSE.txt.
what_it_does: A node in the `falling_node` group starts falling when the cell below is walkable/buildable_to — i.e. when its support disappears — by converting it to a falling entity.
key_api:
core.check_single_for_falling(pos) -> boolean
core.check_for_falling(pos)       -- walks neighbours
core.spawn_falling_node(pos)
-- node opt-in: groups = { falling_node = 1 }
snippet:
function core.check_single_for_falling(p)
	local n = core.get_node(p)
	if core.get_item_group(n.name, "falling_node") ~= 0 then
		local p_bottom = vector.offset(p, 0, -1, 0)
		-- Only spawn falling node if node below is loaded
		local n_bottom = core.get_node_or_nil(p_bottom)
		local d_bottom = n_bottom and core.registered_nodes[n_bottom.name]
		if d_bottom then
			local same = n.name == n_bottom.name
			-- Let leveled nodes fall if it can merge with the bottom node
			if same and d_bottom.paramtype2 == "leveled" and
					core.get_node_level(p_bottom) <
					core.get_node_max_level(p_bottom) then
				local success, _ = convert_to_falling_node(p, n)
				return success
input_output: Input: node position in a voxel grid. Output: boolean; side effect: node removed and a `__builtin:falling_node` entity spawned above.
why_critical_for_this_project: damage-cascade: the published rule for 'a cell falls when its support disappears'. It replaces ad-hoc cascades with a tested support predicate (bottom cell not walkable / buildable_to) and a falling-entity conversion.
maturity_evidence: Luanti 5.17.0 (formerly Minetest), a long-running open-source voxel engine; falling-node behaviour is part of its default game; LGPL-2.1+.
integration_note: Reimplement the 15-line predicate in JS; LGPL applies only if the Lua code is ported/copied, so a clean-room implementation of the rule avoids it. The algorithm is a grid support check, not a physics engine.
risks: Node grid, not continuous physics; falling entity is visual and lands later; only checks the cell below (not lateral support); LGPL if copied; Lua.

name: pixelmatch perceptual pixel diff
licence: ISC (LICENSE: 'ISC License Copyright (c) 2025, Mapbox').
what_it_does: Compares two equally sized RGBA images pixel by pixel with an OKLab HyAB threshold, anti-aliasing detection, optional diff image and optional N×N windowed diff count.
key_api:
pixelmatch(img1, img2, output, width, height, {
  threshold = 0.1,          // OKLab HyAB, 0..1
  includeAA = false,
  alpha = 0.1,
  aaColor = [255,255,0],
  diffColor = [255,0,0],
  checkerboard = true,
  windowSize = Infinity,
  diffMask = false
}) -> number  // mismatched pixels (or max per-window count)
input_output: Input: two RGBA Uint8Array/Uint8ClampedArray of length w*h*4, optional output buffer. Output: diff count (number) and, if output given, a diff RGBA image.
why_critical_for_this_project: gates: the project's reference gate needs a perceptual, AA-aware pixel comparison, not raw equality. pixelmatch's 0.1 threshold and AA handling are the published defaults to quote in gate premises.
maturity_evidence: Mapbox; v8.0.0; a declared dependency of jest-image-snapshot 5.x (npm metadata, 2026-10-17); the de-facto JS screenshot-diff implementation.
integration_note: Browser and Node ESM; ISC; zero dependencies. It compares rendered frames, so the capture must be a finished frame (see the project's screenshot trap).
risks: v8 threshold is OKLab HyAB, not the older YIQ; AA detection can hide real 1-px differences; requires equal dimensions; output buffer must be RGBA; not a quality metric by itself.

name: scikit-image structural similarity (SSIM)
licence: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt: 'Files: * ... License: BSD-3-Clause').
what_it_does: Mean structural similarity with a uniform or Gaussian window, optional full SSIM map and gradient.
key_api:
structural_similarity(im1, im2, *,
    win_size=None, gradient=False, data_range=None,
    channel_axis=None, gaussian_weights=False, full=False)
snippet:
def structural_similarity(
    im1,
    im2,
    *,
    win_size=None,
    gradient=False,
    data_range=None,
    channel_axis=None,
    gaussian_weights=False,
    full=False,
    **kwargs,
):
input_output: Input: two arrays of the same shape; `data_range` should be 255 for uint8. Output: float SSIM (or (score, map) when full=True).
why_critical_for_this_project: gates: an established reference metric for the whole frame, complementing pixelmatch. It must be called with `data_range=255` and a fixed `win_size` so the premise is printable with the verdict.
maturity_evidence: Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, Simoncelli, 'Image Quality Assessment: From Error Visibility to Structural Similarity', IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 13(4), 2004; scikit-image 0.26.0.
integration_note: Python gate (or a JS port such as ssim.js); BSD-3. Run it in the offline chain, not the browser page.
risks: `data_range` inferred from dtype can be wrong for float images; window size must be odd and smaller than the image; SSIM is not designed for pixel art; global score hides local faults.

name: pHash perceptual hash
licence: BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE: two redistribution conditions, 'THIS SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED ... AS IS').
what_it_does: DCT-based perceptual hash: grayscale resize to 32x32, low-frequency 8x8 DCT, threshold at the median, 64-bit hash.
key_api:
phash(image, hash_size=8, highfreq_factor=4) -> ImageHash
# image: PIL image; img_size = hash_size * highfreq_factor (32)
# ImageHash.distance(other) -> Hamming distance
snippet:
import scipy.fftpack
	img_size = hash_size * highfreq_factor
	image = image.convert('L').resize((img_size, img_size), ANTIALIAS)
	pixels = numpy.asarray(image)
	dct = scipy.fftpack.dct(scipy.fftpack.dct(pixels, axis=0), axis=1)
	dctlowfreq = dct[:hash_size, :hash_size]
	med = numpy.median(dctlowfreq)
	diff = dctlowfreq > med
	return ImageHash(diff)
input_output: Input: PIL image. Output: ImageHash (64 boolean values for 8x8). Hamming distance is an integer 0..64.
why_critical_for_this_project: gates: catches global composition/palette changes that a pixel diff misses and tolerates small AA/palette shifts. It is the right 'is this still the same picture?' gate, not a quality score.
maturity_evidence: pHash from Hacker Factor ('Looks Like It'), implemented by imagehash 4.3.2, the standard Python perceptual-hash package; the repo ships `find_similar_images.py` for duplicate detection.
integration_note: Python gate; port DCT or use a JS perceptual-hash library; BSD-2. Hamming distance threshold must be printed with the verdict.
risks: Resize/AA changes the hash; a palette change can flip bits; 64 bits is small; not a quality metric; scipy FFT dependency.

name: Shannon entropy of an image
licence: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt: 'Files: * ... License: BSD-3-Clause').
what_it_does: Histogram Shannon entropy in bits: -sum(pk log pk) over the image's pixel-value distribution.
key_api:
shannon_entropy(image, base=2) -> float
# body: _, counts = unique(image, return_counts=True)
#       return scipy.stats.entropy(counts, base=base)
input_output: Input: grayscale (M,N) array. Output: float bits (0..log2(number of levels)).
why_critical_for_this_project: gates: a flatness/colour-collapse measure. It is the published form of the project's '116 tones, largest 31%' gate and can be printed alongside the histogram's largest-bin share.
maturity_evidence: Shannon entropy (1948); scikit-image 0.26.0 standard measure; the implementation is a two-line wrapper over `scipy.stats.entropy`.
integration_note: Three lines in JS (histogram + -sum p log p); BSD-3. Use it on the finished frame, not a transient overlay.
risks: Entropy of a quantised image is bounded by log2(palette size); it does not measure spatial flatness; a single dominant tone lowers entropy but may be intentional (sky).

name: mulberry32 seeded PRNG
licence: Public domain (file header: '*License: Public domain. Software licenses are annoying...').
what_it_does: A 32-bit-state PRNG: add 0x6D2B79F5, then two imul avalanche rounds; returns a float in [0,1).
input_output: Input: uint32 seed. Output: closure `() => number`.
why_critical_for_this_project: state: the project already ships these exact constants in src/rng.js. This entry is the provenance and the correctness reference: the constants and the `>>> 0` coercions are quoted from the canonical source.
maturity_evidence: bryc's PRNG page: 'very fast and passes gjrand. best 2^32 state JS PRNG'; the page benchmarks it against sfc32/jsf32/xoshiro; the implementation is widely copied (and already present in this repo).
integration_note: Browser/Node, no dependencies; public domain. Keep the `>>> 0` after addition and the two `Math.imul` rounds exactly.
risks: 32-bit state (2^32 period) is small for large worlds; not cryptographic; JavaScript number coercion can silently break the constants if `|0` is omitted; no jump/stream support.

name: splitmix64 seed expander
version_or_commit: no VCS version; 2015 file header; snapshot fetched 2026-10-17
licence: Public domain / CC0 (header: 'To the extent possible under law, the author has dedicated all copyright ... to the public domain worldwide').
what_it_does: A fixed-increment 64-bit generator used to expand one seed into a full xoshiro state; constants are the golden-ratio increment and two avalanche multipliers.
input_output: Input: 64-bit state (any value). Output: 64-bit value.
why_critical_for_this_project: state: deterministic seed expansion for worlds/levels. Use it to turn one photo hash into the 4x64-bit state xoshiro256** needs, instead of an ad-hoc LCG.
maturity_evidence: Sebastiano Vigna, 2015; header cites the Java 8 SplittableRandom paper (DOI 10.1145/2714064.2660195); the header says it passes BigCrush.
integration_note: Port to BigInt (slow) or two 32-bit halves; public domain. It is a seeder, not the main generator.
risks: 64-bit arithmetic in JS needs BigInt or hi/lo pairs; not cryptographic; the C `static` state is not reentrant; do not use it directly for large streams.

name: xoshiro256** 1.0
version_or_commit: no VCS version; 2018 file header; snapshot fetched 2026-10-17
licence: Public domain / CC0 (header: 'To the extent possible under law, the author has dedicated all copyright ... to the public domain worldwide').
what_it_does: A 256-bit-state, 64-bit-output general-purpose PRNG: `rotl(s[1]*5, 7)*9`, with a 256-bit state update and jump/long-jump functions.
key_api:
uint64_t next(void);   // state: static uint64_t s[4], not all zero
void jump(void);       // 2^128 calls
void long_jump(void);  // 2^192 calls
// seed: fill s[0..3] with splitmix64 output
input_output: Input: 4x64-bit nonzero state. Output: 64-bit value per call; jump functions advance the stream.
why_critical_for_this_project: state: a high-quality deterministic stream for damage cascades and procedural variation, with jump for parallel/independent layers. It replaces one shared Math.random and makes replays exact.
maturity_evidence: Blackman & Vigna, 2018, xoshiro256** 1.0; header: 'passes all tests we are aware of'; reference implementation used across languages; the same authors' xoshiro family is widely deployed.
integration_note: BigInt or 32-bit halves; public domain. Seed via splitmix64; never all-zero. The 64-bit arithmetic is the integration cost.
risks: 64-bit JS cost (BigInt is slow); must not seed all-zero; jump constants are easy to mistype; not cryptographic; output is 64-bit so a float conversion needs care.

name: PCG32 (XSH-RR)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.txt: 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004').
what_it_does: PCG32: a 64-bit LCG state with XSH-RR output permutation; small, fast and statistically strong.
input_output: Input: 64-bit initstate + 64-bit initseq (stream). Output: uint32_t per call.
why_critical_for_this_project: state: a proven seeded generator when a 64-bit state is wanted; a second implementation to cross-check mulberry32 streams and to avoid the 'hand-picked constants' pattern.
maturity_evidence: Melissa O'Neill, 'PCG: A Family of Simple Fast Space-Efficient Statistically Good Algorithms for Random Number Generation' (2014); PCG64 is NumPy's default BitGenerator; Apache-2.0 reference C.
integration_note: BigInt or 32-bit halves; Apache-2.0. The increment must be odd; seed with two values (state, stream).
risks: 64-bit arithmetic in JS; not cryptographic; `initseq` must be odd after the shift; the C API uses a global default RNG if `_r` variants are not used.

name: ONNX Runtime session options for deterministic inference
licence: MIT (LICENSE: 'MIT License').
what_it_does: Controls execution mode, graph optimisation, CPU memory arena, memory pattern, thread counts, and (native) deterministic compute for a session.
snippet:
/** \brief Set whether to use deterministic compute.
   *
   * Default is false. If set to true, this will enable deterministic compute for GPU kernels where possible.
   * Note that this most likely will have a performance cost.
   *
   * \param[in] options
   * \param[in] value
   *
   * \since Version 1.17.
   */
input_output: Input: model bytes + SessionOptions. Output: an InferenceSession whose outputs should be bit-reproducible for the same inputs on the same backend.
why_critical_for_this_project: scene-parse/gates: the segmentation and detector outputs must be identical on every run for the frame gates to mean anything. This entry quotes the published knobs and the deterministic-compute default (false).
maturity_evidence: ONNX Runtime (Microsoft), used by transformers.js and MediaPipe; MIT; `SetDeterministicCompute` documented since 1.17 with 'Default is false'; the JS SessionOptions interface is published in the API docs.
integration_note: Browser WASM; MIT. `executionMode`, `graphOptimizationLevel`, `enableCpuMemArena`, `enableMemPattern` are supported by the WASM backend; the docs mark `intraOpNumThreads` Node-only, and deterministic compute is a native GPU option, so the browser must pin what it can and test the rest.
risks: ORT Web may ignore or reject options; threading/GPU reductions are not bit-identical; graph optimisation can change numerics; different EPs (WASM/WebGPU) give different results; the JS API does not expose deterministic compute.

name: font8x8 8x8 bitmap font
licence: Public Domain (header: 'License: Public Domain'; derived from IBM VGA public-domain 8x8 fonts).
what_it_does: A 128-glyph ASCII bitmap font: 8 bytes per glyph, one byte per row, each set bit a lit pixel.
input_output: Input: ASCII code 0-127 + row 0-7. Output: 8-bit row mask.
why_critical_for_this_project: hud-text: a zero-dependency 1KB bitmap font for the HUD; it replaces canvas `fillText` with deterministic pixel glyphs that obey the same integer grid as the frame.
maturity_evidence: Derived from IBM's public-domain VGA 8x8 font (header provenance: Marcel Sondaar / IBM public domain); README Encoding states: 'The least significant bit of each byte corresponds to the first pixel in a row'; commit 8e279d2.
integration_note: Copy the 128x8 table into JS or load the header at build time; public domain. Render with the same 1-bit fill rule as the frame.
risks: ASCII only (no Cyrillic, which the project may need for Russian HUD text); 8x8 is fixed; bit order must match the renderer; anti-aliasing must be off.

name: Tiled TMX map format 1.8
licence: TMX specification: CC-BY-SA 3.0 Unported (footer: 'The TMX Map Format by https://www.mapeditor.org is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported License'). Tiled application: GPL-2.0 (LICENSE.GPL).
what_it_does: XML tile-map format: map orientation/size/tile size, layers, and tile data as CSV, base64(+gzip/zlib/zstd) or individual tiles, addressed by global tile IDs.
key_api:
<map version="1.8" tiledversion="..." orientation="orthogonal"
     renderorder="right-down" width="W" height="H"
     tilewidth="TW" tileheight="TH">
  <layer id="1" name="ground" width="W" height="H">
    <data encoding="csv">1,2,3,...</data>
  </layer>
</map>
snippet:
-  **class:** The class of this map (since 1.9, defaults to "").
-  **orientation:** Map orientation. Tiled supports "orthogonal",
   "isometric", "oblique", "staggered" and "hexagonal" (since 0.11).
-  **renderorder:** The order in which tiles on tile layers are rendered.
   Valid values are ``right-down`` (the default), ``right-up``,
   ``left-down`` and ``left-up``. In all cases, the map is drawn
   row-by-row. (only supported for orthogonal maps at the moment)
-  **compressionlevel:** The compression level to use for tile layer data
   (defaults to -1, which means to use the algorithm default).
-  **width:** The map width in tiles.
-  **height:** The map height in tiles.
-  **tilewidth:** The width of a tile.
-  **tileheight:** The height of a tile.
input_output: Input: XML. Output: tile grid(s) of global IDs (gids); gid 0 = empty; high bits are flip flags.
why_critical_for_this_project: state: a published level format so the photo-derived level can be opened, edited and diffed in Tiled instead of living only in a bespoke JSON. It also fixes the tile-size/orientation vocabulary the level generator must emit.
maturity_evidence: Tiled is the standard 2D map editor; TMX 1.8 is its current documented format; many engines/libraries import TMX (the spec links a support list); docs are CC-BY-SA 3.0.
integration_note: Browser DOMParser, no build. The docs are CC-BY-SA 3.0 (attribution/share-alike for copied spec text); Tiled code is GPL-2.0+. An independent parser is not a derivative of the docs.
risks: XML is verbose; gid flip flags are easy to mishandle; TMX has no physics/semantics; the spec's CC-BY-SA applies to copied text, not to an independent parser.

`__cHei` | Int | Grid-based height `__cWid` | Int | Grid-based width `__gridSize` | Int | Grid size `__identifier` | String | Layer definition identifier `__opacity`

Only *Tile layers, Auto-layers*
![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/Added_0.6.0-gray.svg) | Int *(can be `null`)* | The definition UID of corresponding Tileset, if any. `__tilesetRelPath`

Only *Auto-layers*
![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/Added_0.4.0-gray.svg) | Array of [Tile instance](#ldtk-Tile) | An array containing all tiles generated by Auto-layer rules. The array is already sorted in display order (ie. 1st tile is beneath 2nd, which is beneath 3rd etc.).

input_output: Input: 20 numeric parameters. Output: AudioBufferSourceNode (play) or Float32Array samples (buildSamples).
why_critical_for_this_project: audio: replaces hand-written WebAudio envelopes with a published 8-bit SFX synth for hits, breaks and HUD blips; tiny enough for the no-build ESM constraint.
maturity_evidence: ZzFX 1.4.0; the README lists dozens of js13k/itch games using it (Space Huggers, Clawstrike, Cat Survivors, ...); MIT.
